youtube.title: GPT-6 Astra vs Claude Opus 5.5 vs Gemini: Which One Is Actually Worth Paying For?
youtube.description:
Three jobs people actually run every month, priced on GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Grok 4.7 and Gemini 3.8 Flash with the official list prices of September 28, 2026. The winner is not the smartest model, and the video ends with the three-question test that turns this math into yours.

Every price comes from the vendor's own pricing page on the recording date and will change; the formula is on screen so you can redo it with today's numbers. The picks at the end are the owner's opinion, labelled as such. No model was benchmarked here; the only measurement is arithmetic on published prices.

Recorded 2026-09-28.

scenes.chapter: Three price sheets, one month of work

data.title: Which AI is actually **worth paying** for?
data.subtitle: GPT-6 Astra vs Claude Opus 5.5 vs Gemini, priced on three real jobs

lines.text: GPT-6 Astra costs fifty dollars per million output tokens. Claude Opus 5.5 costs twenty. Gemini 3.8 Flash costs under four.
Pick by benchmark and you overpay. Pick by price and you get work you have to redo.
So I took three jobs people actually run every month and priced each one on each model, with the official rates as of today.
The winner is not the smartest model. Here is the math, and the three questions that make it your math.

data.title: Official list prices, per million tokens, 2026-09-28

lines.text: First, the price sheets side by side, read from each company's own pricing page today.
OpenAI's flagship, GPT-6 Astra: ten dollars in, one dollar for cached input, fifty out, per million tokens.
OpenAI's cheaper sibling, GPT-6 Sol: two in, twenty cents cached, ten out.
Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5: four in, twenty cents cached, twenty out.
xAI's Grok 4.7, for prompts under two hundred thousand tokens: two in, fifty cents cached, six out.
Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash: seventy five cents in, seven and a half cents cached, three dollars seventy five out.
Google says that Flash price holds until the end of the year and then doubles. It lists no Pro price for the 3.8 generation yet.

lines.text: Job two is where the money goes: a coding agent working beside you all day, twenty workdays a month.
Every turn it re-reads the whole conversation, so most of its input is cached. Say six hundred thousand fresh tokens a day.
Two point four million cached tokens a day, and a hundred and fifty thousand tokens of output.
Twenty workdays: twelve million fresh, forty eight million cached, three million out. Now the prices bite.

data.title: Job 2: the coding agent, per month

lines.text: Astra: about three hundred forty eight dollars a month. A hundred fifty of that is cache writes, a fee OpenAI lists for its newer models.
Sol, the cheaper OpenAI model: about seventy. Opus 5.5: about one hundred thirty, sixty of it cache writes.
Grok 4.7: about sixty six. Gemini 3.8 Flash: about twenty four. Neither lists a cache write fee, though Google bills hourly cache storage, which I left out.
Same work, almost a fifteen fold price range. This is the job where picking wrong costs you hundreds a month, or a lot of redo.

lines.text: Job three: a support bot. Ten thousand chats a month, three thousand tokens in and three hundred out each. Thirty million in, three million out.
Astra: four hundred fifty. Opus 5.5: one eighty.
Grok 4.7: seventy eight. Gemini Flash: thirty four. Sol lands at ninety.
Notice where the money goes: input. A support bot reads far more than it writes, so the input price matters most.

scenes.chapter: When the expensive model is cheaper

data.title: Add the cost of being wrong

left.heading: Cheap model, plus fixing it
points: One hour a week fixing its mistakes

right.heading: Pricier model, fewer fixes
points: Your hour and your rate decide

lines.text: Now the twist. The bill is not just the API. If the cheap model needs you to fix its work, your time goes on the bill.
Take the coding job on Gemini Flash at twenty four dollars, and suppose it costs you one hour a week of fixing.
At forty dollars an hour, that is about one hundred sixty dollars more, roughly one eighty four in total.
Opus 5.5 at one hundred thirty, with fewer retries, is now the cheaper option. Change the hour or the rate and it flips back.
Those two numbers, the hour and the rate, are mine, as an example. Yours are the ones that count, and only you can measure them.

data.sub: two tries at a low price can cost more than one at a high price

lines.text: The rule behind the twist: retries multiply everything. Two tries at a low price can cost more than one at a high price.
So the real question is never which model is smartest. It is which model's failure rate on your job you can afford, at the lowest price.

scenes.chapter: The three-question test, and my picks

steps.title: What does a wrong answer cost?
steps.detail: Cheap to check, or expensive to undo

steps.title: How many retries do I really do?
Is the cheaper sibling good enough?
steps.detail: Sol, Flash, Grok before Astra or Opus

lines.text: Here is the test I use before paying for any model. Three questions.
One, what does a wrong answer cost? If it is cheap to check, buy cheap. If it is expensive to undo, pay up.
Two, how many retries do I really do? Count them for a week. Most people guess low.
Three, is the cheaper sibling good enough? Every lab sells one: Sol under Astra, Flash under Pro, the smaller Claude models under Opus.

data.title: My picks, as opinion
rows: Opus 5.5 or Sol, then count retries
Cache writes and redo time dominate
Flash or Grok, with a checker

lines.text: My picks, and these are opinions, not measurements. For the daily summary, the cheapest model that reads well; the money is trivial.
For the coding agent, start with Opus 5.5 or Sol and count your retries for a week before you decide.
For the support bot, Flash or Grok with a checking step, because input volume rules that bill.
And I would not switch because a new model topped a chart this week. I switch when my cost, quality or speed actually changes.
